title: Shopping cart
like: the cart on an online store like Amazon
brief: Shoppers browse products, drop things in a cart and come back later from another phone. Browsing is most of the traffic and can be a little old. The cart itself must always show what the shopper just added.

clarify.q: Can the product pages be a little old?
clarify.a: Yes, by a minute or two. A price that changes is fixed at checkout.
No. If someone adds a shirt and the page reloads without it, they leave.

clarify.q: How long does a cart live?
clarify.a: About 30 days. Most carts are never bought (approx.).

notes: Use the write share to estimate peak cart changes.
A cart is a few KB (approx.).

Scored data retention: at least 30 days on active authoritative stores. Copies used only for search or reports can be rebuilt. Local device history and rollup policies still require the separate protocol check.

numbers.label: Cart changes per second at peak
Product views per second at peak

hints: Product pages and the cart have different promises. Which one may be a minute old?
A cache can answer product views. A key-value store keeps each cart under its owner as the key, with no joins needed.
Load balancer, a few servers, a cache for products, a SQL database for the catalog, and a key-value store for carts.

editorial.summary: Most traffic only looks at products, so a cache answers it. Each cart is one small record looked up by its owner, which is exactly what a key-value store does well, so carts never wait on the catalog database.

designs.name: Cache for products, key-value store for carts
designs.why: The cache serves product pages from memory and may be a minute old. Carts live in a key-value store read and written by one key, so adding an item is visible at once and the store grows without effort.

tradeoffs: A longer cache time saves the catalog database but can show an old price. A minute is a good middle.
A key-value store scales carts easily, but you cannot ask it questions like "who has this item in a cart".
Keeping the cart only in the browser is cheap, but it vanishes when the shopper switches device.
Saving carts for 30 days costs a little storage and brings many shoppers back.
editorial.realWorld: Large shops see a few hundred cart changes a second on a normal evening and many times more on a sale day. Carts are usually kept in key-value stores for exactly this reason (approx.).

correctness.prompt: Shopping cart: The same request is delivered twice, and a worker can crash after saving it. What uniqueness constraint and transaction would keep one durable result?
correctness.discussion: Choose a stable business operation id and enforce a unique constraint in the authoritative store. Insert the id, apply the change and save its result in one transaction. A retry returns that result. Recording the id before the change can lose work after a crash; recording it afterwards can apply the change twice. If work continues through a queue, commit an outbox entry in the same transaction and deduplicate at each consumer.

fields.label: The server commits a change, then crashes before replying. The client retries. What happens?
options: Commit the operation id, effect and result atomically; return that result on retry
Record the id first, then apply the change in a separate write
fields.explanation: Recording the id separately can either lose an operation or apply it twice. The effect and deduplication result must commit together.

fields.label: The server acknowledges a write just before its storage fails. Which evidence meets the stated recovery point?
options: A queued backup request with no completed durable copy
A measured replication or backup gap of at most 60 seconds, with a tested replay plan
fields.explanation: A scheduled copy is not a completed copy. Match acknowledgement and recovery to the stated loss boundary.

twist.brief: Demand has settled at about 750 requests/s. The new monthly ceiling is $1962. The original burst reserve now competes with the operating budget. Decide which reserve to keep, then test its failure headroom. All data and recovery promises still apply.

design.name: Smaller workload, measured reserve
design.why: Reduce the paid floor for the quieter workload, preserving the required copies and recovery settings. This design was checked through the full event day.
